claim: Mim1/Mim2 complex is fungi-specific and required for assembly and/or insertion of a subset of mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) proteins including subunits of the main MOM translocase.
source: Assembly and/or insertion of a subset of mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM) proteins, including subunits of the main MOM translocase, require the fungi-specific Mim1/Mim2 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing the fungi-specific nature and function of the Mim1/Mim2 complex.

claim: pATOM36 of trypanosomes is a functional analogue of yeast Mim1/Mim2 complex despite lacking sequence or topological similarity.
source: Here, we show by reciprocal complementation that the MOM protein pATOM36 of trypanosomes is a functional analogue of yeast Mim1/Mim2 complex, even though these proteins show neither sequence nor topological similarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by reciprocal complementation experiments described in the manuscript showing functional rescue.

claim: Expression of pATOM36 rescues almost all growth, mitochondrial biogenesis, and morphology defects in yeast cells lacking Mim1 and/or Mim2.
source: Expression of pATOM36 rescues almost all growth, mitochondrial biogenesis, and morphology defects in yeast cells lacking Mim1 and/or Mim2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from growth assays, protein level measurements, and microscopy shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Co-expression of Mim1 and Mim2 restores the assembly and/or insertion defects of MOM proteins in trypanosomes ablated for pATOM36.
source: Conversely, co-expression of Mim1 and Mim2 restores the assembly and/or insertion defects of MOM proteins in trypanosomes ablated for pATOM36.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing restoration of ATOM complex assembly in pATOM36-depleted cells expressing Mim1/Mim2, as shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 form native-like complexes when heterologously expressed, indicating that additional proteins are not part of these structures.
source: Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 form native-like complexes when heterologously expressed, indicating that additional proteins are not part of these structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by BN-PAGE analysis showing complex formation in heterologous systems (Figures 1B, 6D, 6E).

claim: Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 are products of convergent evolution that arose only after the ancestors of fungi and trypanosomatids diverged.
source: Our findings indicate that Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 are the products of convergent evolution and arose only after the ancestors of fungi and trypanosomatids diverged.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of sequence similarity, different topologies, and phylogenetic distribution of the proteins.

claim: pATOM36 is an integral MOM protein with the C-terminus exposed to the cytosol in T. brucei.
source: In T. brucei, pATOM36 is an integral MOM protein with the C-terminus exposed to the cytosol (Pusnik et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by protease protection assays in the current study (Figure 1A).

claim: Endogenous pATOM36 in T. brucei occurs in two groups of protein complexes with molecular weights of approximately 140–250 kDa and larger than 480 kDa.
source: Blue native (BN)-PAGE analysis has shown that the endogenous protein occurs in two groups of protein complexes of unknown composition with molecular weights of approximately 140–250 kDa and larger than 480 kDa (Käser et al., 2016; Pusnik et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior BN-PAGE analyses.

claim: pATOM36-HA expressed in yeast is accessible to proteinase K in isolated mitochondria, indicating cytosolic exposure of the C-terminal HA tag.
source: We observed that the C-terminally HA-tagged pATOM36, similar to the yeast import receptor Tom70, is accessible to added proteinase K in isolated mitochondria, whereas the matrix protein Hep1 was protected as would be expected for intact organelles (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: pATOM36 expressed in yeast is an integral membrane protein as shown by alkaline extraction.
source: Alkaline extraction of the isolated organelles showed that pATOM36, as Tom70 but unlike the soluble matrix protein Hep1, was detected in the pellet fraction indicating that it is an integral membrane protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by alkaline extraction data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: pATOM36 expressed in yeast forms complexes of similar size to the 140 and 250 kDa complexes observed in T. brucei mitochondria.
source: Finally, a BN-PAGE analysis demonstrated that pATOM36 expressed in yeast forms complexes of similar size to the 140 and 250 kDa complexes observed in T. brucei mitochondria (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The higher molecular weight pATOM36 complex (>480 kDa) observed in T. brucei was not detected when pATOM36 was expressed in yeast.
source: However, the higher molecular weight complex, which likely corresponds to a TAC subcomplex required for kDNA maintenance (Käser et al., 2016), was not detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of the high molecular weight complex in BN-PAGE analysis (Figure 1B) and inference about its TAC-related function.

claim: pATOM36 and pATOM36-HA can rescue the growth defect on respiratory carbon sources of mim1Δ or mim2Δ yeast cells.
source: Under all the tested conditions, pATOM36 and pATOM36-HA were able to rescue the growth defect caused by the absence of either Mim1 or Mim2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by drop dilution assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The rescue capacity of pATOM36 is similar to that of Mim1 or Mim2 in the corresponding deletion strains.
source: Of note, the rescue capacity of pATOM36 was similar to that of Mim1 or Mim2 in the corresponding deletion strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of growth rescue in drop dilution assays (Figure 2A).

claim: pATOM36 can functionally compensate for the absence of both Mim1 and Mim2 in yeast double deletion cells.
source: We observed that pATOM36 could functionally compensate for the absence of both Mim1 and Mim2, since it was able to rescue the growth defect on non-fermentable carbon sources, a condition which requires fully functional mitochondria (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Absence of Mim1 and/or Mim2 in yeast cells results in reduction in the steady-state levels of MOM proteins Ugo1, Tom20 and Tom70.
source: The absence of Mim1 and/or Mim2 in yeast cells results in a variety of mitochondrial defects including reduction in the steady-state levels of Mim1/2 substrates like the outer membrane proteins Ugo1, Tom20 and Tom70 (Dimmer et al., 2012; Ishikawa et al., 2004; Popov-Celeketić et al., 2008; Waizenegger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Expression of pATOM36-HA restores the levels of Tom20 and Tom70 in mitochondria from mim1Δ/mim2Δ double deletion cells.
source: The results indicate that, whereas expression of pATOM36-HA in WT cells did not alter the abundance of the tested proteins or did it only to a minor extent, it did restore the levels of Mim1/2 substrates Tom20 and Tom70 in mitochondria from the double deletion cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The effect of pATOM36 on the levels of Ugo1 was only marginal, suggesting that pATOM36 has preferences to certain MIM substrates.
source: Interestingly, the effect of pATOM36 on the levels of Ugo1 was only marginal, suggesting that pATOM36 has preferences to certain MIM substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data (Figure 3A, 3B) and represents an inference about substrate specificity.

claim: Cells lacking Mim1/2 accumulate mitochondrial precursor proteins due to hampered assembly of the TOM complex.
source: A further phenotype of cells lacking Mim1/2 is the accumulation of mitochondrial precursor proteins due to hampered assembly of the TOM complex (Ishikawa et al., 2004; Mnaimneh et al., 2004; Waizenegger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The presence of pATOM36-HA in mim1Δ/mim2Δ deletion strains completely eliminated the appearance of the precursor form of mitochondrial Hsp60.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3C, the presence of pATOM36-HA in the deletion strains completely eliminated the appearance of the precursor form of mitochondrial Hsp60.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence of pATOM36-HA in mim1Δ/mim2Δ deletion cell lines resulted in enhanced levels of Tom40.
source: The presence of pATOM36-HA in the deletion cell lines resulted also in enhanced levels of Tom40 whereas the amounts of aconitase (Aco1) were not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of Mim1/2, there is a dramatic reduction in the amount of assembled TOM complex and an appearance of an unassembled Tom40-containing species.
source: As expected, in the absence of Mim1/2, a dramatic reduction in the amount of assembled TOM complex and an appearance of an unassembled Tom40-containing species can be observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Introduction of pATOM36-HA into mim1Δ/mim2Δ cells completely reverses the alterations in TOM complex assembly caused by the absence of Mim1/2.
source: Strikingly, these alterations completely disappeared upon the introduction of pATOM36-HA into these cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: pATOM36 cannot functionally replace Mas37/Sam37, a subunit of the TOB/SAM complex.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows that pATOM36 could revert neither the drop in the steady-state levels of the TOB complex and its altered assembly behaviour nor the reduced levels of either the β-barrel proteins Tom40 and Porin or the single-span protein Tom22.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of pATOM36 is specific for MIM substrates.
source: Thus, the effect of pATOM36 is specific for MIM substrates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the inability of pATOM36 to complement Mas37/Sam37 deletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The single-span protein Tom22 follows an import pathway that is distinct from that taken by the signal-anchored subunits Tom20 and Tom70.
source: These findings further support the notion that the single-span protein Tom22 follows an import pathway that is distinct from that taken by the signal-anchored subunits Tom20 and Tom70.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of pATOM36 on different MOM proteins.

claim: Tom70 works together with Mim1 in the biogenesis of multi-span helical MOM proteins.
source: Previous reports suggested that Tom70 works together with Mim1 in the biogenesis of multi-span helical MOM proteins (Becker et al., 2011; Papic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: pATOM36 can interact with the cytosolic domain of Tom70 (GST-Tom70).
source: When this protein was incubated with newly synthesised radiolabelled pATOM36, or with Mim1 as a control, we observed a specific binding to both proteins (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by GST-pulldown data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: pATOM36 may cooperate with Tom70 in the biogenesis of MOM proteins, similarly to Mim1.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that Tom70, as an import receptor for MOM proteins, recognises Mim1 and pATOM36 as substrates, it can be envisaged that, similarly to Mim1, pATOM36 can also cooperate with Tom70 in the biogenesis of MOM proteins.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the interaction data and analogy to Mim1.

claim: The presence of pATOM36 in mitochondria lacking Mim1/2 dramatically improves the capacity to import radiolabelled Tom20 molecules.
source: This assay clearly demonstrated that the presence of pATOM36 is sufficient to improve dramatically the capacity of organelles lacking Mim1/2 to import radiolabelled Tom20 molecules (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in vitro import assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The assembly of newly synthesised Tom20 molecules into pre-existing TOM complexes was markedly improved when pATOM36 was present in mitochondria lacking the MIM complex.
source: Along the same line, the assembly of newly synthesised Tom20 molecules into pre-existing TOM complexes was markedly improved when pATOM36 was present in mitochondria lacking the MIM complex (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by BN-PAGE import assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of pATOM36 did not improve the capacity of isolated mitochondria to import radiolabelled Ugo1.
source: Similarly to its minor effect on the steady state levels of Ugo1, the presence of pATOM36 did not improve the capacity of isolated mitochondria to import radiolabelled Ugo1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in vitro import assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: pATOM36 did not alter the import of the matrix-targeted model protein pSu9-DHFR or the MOM tail-anchored protein Fis1.
source: In both cases, we did not observe altered import upon expression of pATOM36 (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in vitro import assay data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: pATOM36 can support the biogenesis of MIM substrates but appears to have preferences to certain ones.
source: Collectively, pATOM36 can support the biogenesis of MIM substrates but appears to have preferences to certain ones.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of pATOM36 on different MIM substrates (Tom20 vs. Ugo1).

claim: pATOM36 is able to revert the mitochondrial fragmentation observed in cells lacking Mim1 and/or Mim2 to the tubular-like morphology of organelles in control cells.
source: Analysis of mitochondria from the resulting cell lines by fluorescence microscopy revealed that pATOM36 is able to revert the mitochondrial fragmentation observed in cells lacking Mim1 and/or Mim2 to the tubular-like morphology of organelles in control cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Both Mim1-myc and Mim2-HA are expressed and exclusively localised in the mitochondrial fraction when expressed in T. brucei.
source: Subcellular fractionation of induced cells showed that both proteins are expressed and, like the mitochondrial marker protein ATOM40, they are exclusively localised in the mitochondrial fraction (Figure 6B, top panels).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mim1 and Mim2 expressed in T. brucei are integral membrane proteins.
source: Alkaline extraction of the latter revealed that, as the endogenous proteins in yeast, both Mim1 and Mim2 are recovered in the pellet, together with the integral membrane protein ATOM40, whereas the soluble protein CytC was present in the supernatant (Figure 6B, lower panels).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by alkaline extraction data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mim1 and Mim2 acquired their native topology in T. brucei mitochondria with their N-terminus exposed to the cytosol and the C-terminus located in the IMS.
source: Thus, Mim1 and Mim2 acquired their native topology in T. brucei mitochondria with their N-terminus exposed to the cytosol and the C-terminus located in the IMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data showing formation of C-terminal protease-resistant fragments (Figure 6C).

claim: Mim1 and Mim2 of yeast cells form a complex of approximately 200 kDa.
source: Mim1 and Mim2 of yeast cells form a complex of approx. 200 kDa (Dimmer et al., 2012; Ishikawa et al., 2004; Waizenegger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Complexes of ca. 230 kDa containing both Mim1-myc and Mim2-HA can be detected in T. brucei.
source: BN-PAGE shows that similar complexes of ca. 230 kDa, which contain both Mim1-myc and Mim2-HA, could be detected in T. brucei (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mim1/Mim2 complexes in T. brucei migrate similarly to complexes harbouring Mim1-HA and Mim2-HA of yeast mitochondria.
source: Importantly, these complexes migrated similarly to complexes harbouring Mim1-HA and Mim2-HA of yeast mitochondria (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by comparative BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The slightly higher molecular weight of Mim1/Mim2 complexes in T. brucei compared to native yeast complexes can be explained by the fact that both proteins are tagged.
source: The slightly higher molecular weight than that observed for native complexes in yeast can be explained by the fact that both proteins are tagged.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known molecular weight contribution of epitope tags.

claim: Expression of Mim1 and Mim2 results in a native-like MIM complex in mitochondria from T. brucei.
source: Thus, expression of Mim1 and Mim2 results in a native-like MIM complex in mitochondria from T. brucei.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the topology, localization, and complex formation data (Figure 6).

claim: Ablation of pATOM36 causes a growth arrest in T. brucei.
source: Ablation of pATOM36 has been shown to cause a growth arrest.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by growth curve data (Figure 7A).

claim: The lack of pATOM36 interferes with the assembly and/or insertion of MOM proteins and prevents assembly of the TAC, which causes loss of the kDNA.
source: Due to its dual function the lack of pATOM36 does not only interfere with the assembly and/or insertion of MOM proteins but it also prevents assembly of the TAC, which causes loss of the kDNA (Figure 7A) (Käser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and kDNA loss data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Introducing Mim1/2 into pATOM36-depleted cells could not prevent the loss of kDNA but it did cause a milder growth phenotype.
source: Interestingly, introducing Mim1/2 into the pATOM36-depleted cells could not prevent the loss of kDNA but it did cause a milder growth phenotype (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by growth and kDNA loss data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The steady-state levels of ATOM complex subunits ATOM46, ATOM19, and ATOM14 are greatly reduced in the absence of pATOM36.
source: When mitochondrial proteins from pATOM36-depleted cells expressing Mim1/2 were analysed, we observed that the steady-state levels of the ATOM complex subunits ATOM46, ATOM19, and ATOM14, all of which are greatly reduced in the absence of pATOM36, were restored (Figure 7B) (Käser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of Mim1/2 in pATOM36-depleted cells restores the steady-state levels of ATOM complex subunits ATOM46, ATOM19, and ATOM14.
source: When mitochondrial proteins from pATOM36-depleted cells expressing Mim1/2 were analysed, we observed that the steady-state levels of the ATOM complex subunits ATOM46, ATOM19, and ATOM14, all of which are greatly reduced in the absence of pATOM36, were restored (Figure 7B) (Käser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In pATOM36-depleted cells expressing Mim1/2, ATOM subunits are incorporated into high-molecular-weight ATOM complexes.
source: Furthermore, not only the abundance of the ATOM subunits was back to normal levels, but also the subunits were incorporated into the high-molecular-weight ATOM complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In cell lines complemented by the MIM complex, the ATOM subunit complexes were shifted to a slightly higher molecular weight.
source: Of note, in the cell lines complemented by the MIM complex the ATOM subunit complexes were shifted to a slightly higher molecular weight (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Complementation of the ATOM40-containing complexes by Mim1/2 was somewhat incomplete, since the 200 kDa ATOM40 complexes that accumulate after ablation of pATOM36 were still visible.
source: Moreover, complementation of the ATOM40-containing complexes was somewhat incomplete, since the 200 kDa ATOM40 complexes that accumulate after ablation of pATOM36 were still visible (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by BN-PAGE data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Ablation of pATOM36 in trypanosomes causes a condensation of the network-like structure of the trypanosomal mitochondrion.
source: It has previously been described that ablation of pATOM36 in trypanosomes, reminiscent to deletion of the MIM complex in yeast, causes a condensation of the network-like structure of the trypanosomal mitochondrion (Bruggisser et al., 2017) (Figure 8B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the presence of the MIM complex, the mitochondrial morphology phenotype caused by pATOM36 ablation is reversed and the wild type morphology is fully restored.
source: The immunofluorescence analysis in the right panel of Figure 8B indicates that in the presence of the MIM complex also this phenotype is reversed and the wild type morphology of the mitochondrion is fully restored.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Mim1/2 can replace the function of endogenous pATOM36 in MOM protein biogenesis in trypanosomes.
source: Hence, similarly to the rescue capacity of pATOM36 in yeast cells, Mim1/2 can replace the function of endogenous pATOM36 in MOM protein biogenesis in trypanosomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the restoration of ATOM complex assembly and mitochondrial morphology (Figures 7B, 8A, 8B).

claim: Expression of Mim1 or Mim2 alone cannot complement for the protein biogenesis phenotype caused by the lack of pATOM36.
source: Most importantly, both cell lines show a strong deficiency of ATOM complex assembly (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, top panels) and a growth arrest (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, bottom graphs) that are indistinguishable from the parent pATOM36-RNAi cell line (Figure 8A, left panels and Figure 7, left graph, respectively). This indicates that expression of Mim1 or Mim2 alone cannot complement for the protein biogenesis phenotype caused by the lack of pATOM36.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Successful complementation of pATOM36 function requires similar amounts of Mim1 and Mim2.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that successful complementation requires similar amounts of Mim1 and Mim2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure of complementation when only one Mim protein is predominantly expressed (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: The MIM complex of yeast and trypanosomal pATOM36 have identical functions despite not sharing sequence similarity, the same membrane topology, or a similar size.
source: Our study shows that the MIM complex of yeast, consisting of Mim1 and Mim2, and trypanosomal pATOM36 have identical functions, even though they do not share sequence similarity, the same membrane topology, or a similar size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the reciprocal complementation data and comparison of protein features shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The role of pATOM36 in mitochondrial DNA inheritance in trypanosomes cannot be carried out by the MIM complex.
source: The only major limitation is that the role of pATOM36 in mitochondrial DNA inheritance in trypanosomes cannot be carried out by the MIM complex, which is expected since unlike the MIM complex pATOM36 has a dual function (Käser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the kDNA loss data (Figure 7A) and citation to prior work on pATOM36's dual function.

claim: Yeast belongs to the eukaryotic supergroup of the Opisthokonts whereas trypanosomes are Excavates.
source: The reciprocal complementation is surprising because yeast belongs to the eukaryotic supergroup of the Opisthokonts whereas trypanosomes are Excavates (Burki, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to phylogenetic classification.

claim: The MIM complex and pATOM36 evolved after the eukaryotic supergroups were already established.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for the observed phylogenetic distribution of the two functional analogues is that the MIM complex and pATOM36 evolved after the eukaryotic supergroups were already established.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution and lack of homology between the proteins.

claim: Within the Opisthokonts, the MIM complex is restricted to fungi.
source: Moreover, the observation that within the Opisthokonts the MIM complex is restricted to fungi suggests that it evolved only after the divergence of the ancestors of fungi and metazoans.
evidence: This claim is based on phylogenetic distribution knowledge.

claim: The last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) likely did not contain the MIM complex, pATOM36 or any other functional analogue of these proteins.
source: Thus, the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) likely did not contain the MIM complex, pATOM36 or any other functional analogue of these proteins.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution and convergent evolution of the proteins.

claim: LECA had a much simpler MOM protein import system consisting possibly only of a Tom40-like β-barrel protein.
source: This assumption is in line with the notion that LECA had a much simpler MOM protein import system consisting possibly only of a Tom40-like β-barrel protein (Dolezal et al., 2006; Mani et al., 2016), whose integration into the MOM is mediated by the TOB/SAM complex, the core subunit of which, Tob55/Sam50, is conserved in all eukaryotes (Dolezal et al., 2006; Gentle et al., 2004; Kozjak et al., 2003; Paschen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on mitochondrial evolution.

claim: During evolution, additional subunits that are anchored in the membrane by α-helices joined the TOM complex to increase its specificity and efficiency.
source: During evolution, additional subunits that are anchored in the membrane by α-helices joined the TOM complex to increase its specificity and efficiency.
evidence: This claim is an inference about mitochondrial evolution based on comparative analysis.

claim: The TOM complexes of yeast, plants and trypanosomes contain three distinct evolutionary unrelated pairs of protein import receptors.
source: This scenario is supported by the fact that the TOM complexes of yeast, plants and trypanosomes, representatives of three different eukaryotic supergroups, contain three distinct evolutionary unrelated pairs of protein import receptors (Mani et al., 2015; Mani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: The appearance of new TOM subunits required the evolution of a system, such as the MIM complex or pATOM36, that facilitates their assembly with Tom40.
source: The appearance of the new TOM subunits required the evolution of a system, such as the MIM complex or pATOM36, that facilitates their assembly with Tom40.
evidence: This claim is an inference about evolutionary necessity based on the functional data.

claim: The capacity of pATOM36 expressed in yeast cells to support the biogenesis of MIM substrates is variable with Tom20 as the most favourable substrate and Ugo1 as the least favourable one.
source: Interestingly, the capacity of pATOM36 expressed in yeast cells to support the biogenesis of MIM substrates is variable with the import receptor Tom20 as the most favourable substrate and the fusion-modulator Ugo1 as the least favourable one.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential rescue effects observed in steady-state levels and import assays (Figures 3, 4).

claim: Ugo1 is a carrier-like protein with several TMSs that lack clear homologues in higher eukaryotes.
source: Ugo1 is a carrier-like protein with several TMSs that lack clear homologues in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Ugo1.

claim: pATOM36 cannot deal well with Ugo1 since there are no similar substrates in the MOM of T. brucei.
source: Hence, one can speculate that pATOM36 cannot deal with it well since there are no similar substrates in the MOM of T. brucei.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the substrate specificity data and comparative analysis.

claim: Both Mim1 and Mim2 as well as pATOM36 occur in protein complexes of unknown composition.
source: Both Mim1 and Mim2 as well as pATOM36 occur in protein complexes of unknown composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by BN-PAGE data showing complex formation (Figures 1B, 6D).

claim: The MIM complex and pATOM36 complexes do not contain any additional proteins beyond Mim1/Mim2 or pATOM36 oligomers.
source: The successful complementation experiments together with the fact that they form complexes of similar sizes when expressed in the heterologous systems strongly suggest that these complexes do not contain any additional proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the successful heterologous complementation and complex formation data.

claim: The essential function of Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 does not require any further proteins.
source: Their ability for reciprocal rescue also suggests that their essential function does not require any further proteins since it is very unlikely that such factors would be present in the other species.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reciprocal complementation data.

claim: Mim1 and Mim2 have each a single TMS with the N-terminus facing the cytosol.
source: However, whereas Mim1 and Mim2 have each a single TMS with the N-terminus facing the cytosol, the topology of pATOM36 is largely unknown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Mim1/Mim2 topology.

claim: The topology of pATOM36 is largely unknown.
source: However, whereas Mim1 and Mim2 have each a single TMS with the N-terminus facing the cytosol, the topology of pATOM36 is largely unknown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim acknowledges the uncertainty in pATOM36 topology prediction.

claim: The C-terminus of pATOM36 is exposed to the cytosol as demonstrated by antibody shift experiments.
source: It has been demonstrated by antibody shift experiments that the C-terminus of pATOM36 is exposed to the cytosol (Pusnik et al., 2012), but depending on the prediction programs the protein is postulated to have either one, two or even three TMSs (Käser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Depending on prediction programs, pATOM36 is postulated to have either one, two or even three TMSs.
source: It has been demonstrated by antibody shift experiments that the C-terminus of pATOM36 is exposed to the cytosol (Pusnik et al., 2012), but depending on the prediction programs the protein is postulated to have either one, two or even three TMSs (Käser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior computational predictions.

claim: Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 all have GxxxG(A) motifs within their putative TMSs.
source: While Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 do not share sequence similarity and also have different molecular weights (Mim1, 13 kDa; Mim2, 11 kDa; pATOM36, 36 kDa), they all have GxxxG(A) motifs within their putative TMSs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is in line with their oligomeric quaternary structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of GxxxG(A) motifs in Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 is in line with their oligomeric quaternary structures.
source: While Mim1/Mim2 and pATOM36 do not share sequence similarity and also have different molecular weights (Mim1, 13 kDa; Mim2, 11 kDa; pATOM36, 36 kDa), they all have GxxxG(A) motifs within their putative TMSs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is in line with their oligomeric quaternary structures.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on known structural biology principles about GxxxG motifs promoting helix-helix interactions.

claim: Mim1, on its own or in complex with Mim2, can form a cation-selective channel as shown by electrophysiological experiments.
source: It has recently been shown by electrophysiological experiments that Mim1, on its own or in complex with Mim2, can form a cation-selective channel (Krüger et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior electrophysiological work.

claim: If the channel activity of Mim1 is functionally relevant, pATOM36 would be expected to form also a pore.
source: Should this channel activity of Mim1 be functionally relevant, we would expect pATOM36 to form also a pore.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the functional analogy between Mim1 and pATOM36.

claim: It is unclear whether the convergent evolution of the MIM complex and pATOM36 resulted in a similar 3D-structure of the two oligomers.
source: Presently, it is unclear whether the convergent evolution of the MIM complex and pATOM36 demonstrated in the present study, resulted in a similar 3D-structure of the two oligomers.
evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty about structural similarity.

claim: If the MIM complex and pATOM36 have similar 3D-structures, they may independently have evolved the same mechanisms to perform equivalent functions.
source: Should this be the case, the two complexes may independently have evolved the same mechanisms to perform the equivalent functions.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential mechanistic similarity.

claim: The MIM complex and pATOM36 may use structurally different solutions resulting in different mechanisms that nevertheless allow them to carry out the same functions.
source: Alternatively, it cannot be excluded that they use structurally different solutions resulting in different mechanisms that nevertheless allow them to carry out the same functions.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential mechanistic differences.

claim: There is evidence that both the yeast MIM complex and trypanosomal pATOM36 mediate assembly of already integrated MOM proteins and at least for some substrates also the insertion process itself.
source: There is evidence that both the yeast MIM complex as well as trypanosomal pATOM36 mediate assembly of already integrated MOM proteins and at least for some substrates also the insertion process itself (Becker et al., 2008a; Becker et al., 2011; Bruggisser et al., 2017; Dimmer et al., 2012; Hulett et al., 2008; Käser et al., 2016; Lueder and Lithgow, 2009; Papic et al., 2011; Thornton et al., 2010; Waizenegger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: It is unclear whether the MIM complex and pATOM36 directly catalyse protein insertion or whether they form microdomains in the MOM that facilitate membrane integration of helical segments.
source: Whether the two oligomers directly catalyse protein insertion or whether they form microdomains in the MOM that facilitate membrane integration of helical segments is unclear.
evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism of action.

claim: The MIM complex and pATOM36 should behave similarly with respect to their mechanism of facilitating protein insertion.
source: In any case, we hypothesise that the MIM complex and pATOM36 should behave similarly in this respect.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on their functional equivalence.
